source_text:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε ταῖς ἑτεροδοξίαις μηδὲ μυθεύμασιν τοῖς παλαιοῖς ἀνωφελέσιν οὖσιν. εἰ γὰρ μέχρι νῦν κατὰ Ἰουδαῖσμὸν ζῶμεν, ὁμολογοῦμεν χάριν μὴ εἰληφέναι.
οἱ γὰρ θειότατοι προφῆται κατὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν ἔζησαν. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἐδιώχθησαν, ἐνπνεόμενοι ὑπὸ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ, εἰς τὸ πληροφορηθῆναι τοὺς ἀπειθοῦντας, ὅτι εἶς θεός ἐστιν, ὁ φανερώσας ἑαυτὸν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ὅς ἐστιν αὐτοῦ λόγος ἁπὸ σιγῆς προελθών, ὃς κατὰ πάντα εὐηρέστησεν τῷ πέμψαντι αὐτόν.
thought_title: The prophets lived by Christ, not by Judaism
orientation: Ignatius is warning the Magnesians against false teachings and old myths, arguing that even the ancient prophets lived according to Jesus Christ.
pass_a_gloss: Do not be led astray by the heterodox opinions nor by old myths, which are useless. For if until now according to Judaism we live, we confess grace not to have received. For the most divine prophets according to Christ Jesus lived. Because of this also they were persecuted, being inspired by his grace, so that the disobedient might be fully convinced that one God is, the one who revealed himself through Jesus Christ his Son, who is his Word, from silence having come forth, who in all things pleased the one who sent him.

lemmas.gloss: to be fully convinced, to be fully assured

choices.why: The glossary uses 'false teaching' for αἵρεσις; ἑτεροδοξία is a different word meaning heterodox opinions, but 'false teachings' is clearer for a first-time reader and avoids the technical term.
The adjective παλαιοῖς modifies μυθεύμασιν directly; 'old myths' is the natural English order and keeps the dismissive tone.
The glossary gives 'Judaism' for Ἰουδαϊσμός; the phrase κατὰ Ἰουδαῖσμὸν means living by Jewish practice, which Ignatius rejects.

choices.english: we are admitting that we have not received grace
choices.why: ὁμολογοῦμεν here means 'we confess/admit' a negative fact; the perfect infinitive εἰληφέναι keeps the completed sense of not having received.
rejected: we confess grace not to have received
we acknowledge we have not received grace

choices.why: λόγος is a title for Christ here; 'Word' is capitalized to mark it as a title. προελθών is an aorist participle meaning 'having come forth,' rendered as 'coming forth' for natural English.
The verb εὐαρεστέω means 'to be well-pleasing to'; 'pleased' captures the sense that Christ was fully acceptable to the Father who sent him.

pass_b_english: Do not be led astray by false teachings or by old myths, which are worthless. For if we still live according to Judaism, we are admitting that we have not received grace.

The most divine prophets lived according to Christ Jesus. That is why they were persecuted: they were inspired by his grace so that the disobedient might be fully convinced that there is one God, who revealed himself through Jesus Christ his Son, who is his Word, who came forth from silence, and who in every way pleased the one who sent him.

last_rejected.why: μυθεύμασιν means 'myths/fables' but context suggests Jewish oral traditions, not Greek myths; 'old fables' or 'old tales' better.
last_rejected.ruling: μυθεύμασιν means myths/fables; 'myths' is within normal range. Contextual preference for 'tales' is not a major error.

last_rejected.why: πληροφορηθῆναι means 'to be fully informed/assured,' but here passive with τοὺς ἀπειθοῦντας as object of the prophets' mission: 'to convince the disobedient.'
last_rejected.ruling: πληροφορηθῆναι with τοὺς ἀπειθοῦντας naturally means 'fully convince/persuade the disobedient'; 'fully convinced' captures this meaning adequately.

problems.quote: who is his Word coming forth from silence
problems.why: Theological phrase 'coming forth from silence' is obscure in English; may read as word salad.
problems.fix: Add note or rephrase: 'his Word who emerged from hiddenness/silence.'

edits.old: who is his Word coming forth from silence
edits.new: who is his Word, who came forth from silence

fixed: Rephrased 'coming forth from silence' to 'who came forth from silence' to clarify the relative clause structure; the source reads ὃς... προελθών, 'who... having come forth,' so the English now reflects the participial clause more clearly without changing the meaning.
